title: State of the U.S. Chicken Restaurant Industry — 2026
dek: Category growth has halved in two years. Growth is no longer being created; it is being redistributed.

sections.p: Chicken chain sales grew 5.3% in 2025, down from 9.1% in 2024 and more than 12% in 2023. That is still meaningfully ahead of the 3% posted by the restaurant industry overall, and the demand backdrop remains excellent — USDA projects per-capita chicken availability at a record 102.8 pounds in 2026, keeping chicken the most consumed animal protein in America. What has changed is that the category is no longer growing fast enough for every brand to win.

Dave's Hot Chicken grew sales 51% and units 52.3% in 2025, making it the fastest-growing chain among the 200 largest concepts in America. Raising Cane's added 10.3% more units and 10.6% more sales, crossing $5.48B. Layne's Chicken Fingers doubled its footprint for a second consecutive year. Zaxby's crossed 1,000 units. Every one of those gains came out of somebody else's traffic.

KFC closed 312 U.S. restaurants in the twelve months to July 2026 — 7.64% of its American footprint — and ended 2025 at 3,523 units against 3,669 entering the year. Popeyes has now posted six consecutive quarters of negative U.S. comparable sales, with Q1 2026 at -6.5%, its worst quarter in roughly two decades. Jollibee closed more than 200 stores group-wide in the first half of 2026 and cut its opening target. Even Wingstop, the category's development champion, saw domestic same-store sales fall 7.5% in Q2 2026.

sections.h: The franchisee is where it breaks first
sections.p: Restaurant Brands International disclosed that average Popeyes franchisee restaurant-level profitability fell to roughly $235,000 in 2025. Within weeks, Sailormen — a 136-restaurant operator with 3,300 employees and $233.5M of fiscal 2025 revenue — filed Chapter 11. Ninety-seven restaurants sold for $16.55M total across five buyers, and roughly 33 more went dark through lease rejection. Brand-level metrics did not predict that. Operator-level economics did.

For 2027, the category's most important variable is not consumer demand for chicken — that is secure. It is whether the brands losing share can stabilize franchisee unit economics before their operators run out of balance sheet. KFC is furthest along: three consecutive quarters of positive comps after seven negative ones, a menu reset around boneless, wings and sauces, and a U.S. headquarters move to Texas. Popeyes is earliest: a new U.S. president out of the Burger King turnaround, a narrowed menu, permanent value architecture, and a field organization expanding roughly 75%.

title: Chicken QSR Real Estate Report — 2026
dek: A 100 basis point spread now separates corporate from franchisee credit. That spread is the whole business.

sections.p: Corporate-guaranteed QSR cap rates rose three basis points to 5.85% in Q2 2026 while franchisee-guaranteed QSR rose five basis points to 6.85%. Overall single-tenant net lease sat at 6.80% with retail at 6.55%. Premium ground lease product for McDonald's and Chick-fil-A asked the lowest cap rates in the sector at roughly 4.45%.

sections.h: The top of the market keeps setting records
sections.p: In July 2026 a new-construction Chick-fil-A in Hixson, Tennessee traded at $2.77M and a 4.15% cap rate — per CoStar the lowest cap rate ever achieved on a single-tenant Chick-fil-A drive-thru in the state, and achieved on a 15-year term rather than the customary 20. Raising Cane's corporate-guaranteed ground leases price at 4.70%–5.00%, with a $6.84M transaction closing at 4.75%. Two brands in this category now price like credit instruments rather than restaurants.

sections.h: The bottom of the market is repricing
sections.p: Popeyes assets are marketed between 5.10% and 6.80% with an average asking cap rate near 5.80%, on 15–20 year terms with 7.5%–10% escalations. But the credit behind most of those leases is a franchisee, and 2026 supplied a live demonstration of what that means: a 136-unit Popeyes operator filed Chapter 11 and rejected roughly 33 leases. Short-term, non-rated restaurant tenants can trade 200 to 300 basis points wider than premium ground leases — and that gap widens when the operator's comps are negative.

Single-tenant property supply jumped 12.5% quarter over quarter in Q2 2026 to nearly 5,800 available properties, with retail listings up 16.2%. Layered on top of that is genuine second-generation chicken inventory: 312 KFC closures in twelve months, roughly 33 rejected Popeyes leases in Florida and Georgia, 12 Church's units ceasing operations in 2025, and roughly 30 Hooters pads closing in a single day in June 2025.

The opportunity in chicken real estate in 2026–2027 is not buying a 4.15% Chick-fil-A ground lease. It is the second-generation inventory: freestanding drive-thru boxes in trade areas that have supported chicken for thirty years, coming to market through franchisee distress and brand rationalization rather than through a marketed process. That inventory is generated by operator failure, which is why an operator database is a real estate tool.

title: The U.S. Chicken Franchisee Landscape — 2026
dek: One operator controls a quarter of the KFC system. Another 136-unit operator ceased to exist in eleven months.

sections.p: KBP Brands reached 1,224 total units in 2026, up from 1,119 in 2025, and remains the nation's largest KFC franchisee at 831 locations — roughly a quarter of the entire U.S. KFC system. KBP has also diversified beyond Yum! Brands, adding 119 Arby's and 167 Sonic units across two rounds. Ampex Brands runs roughly 600 units with about $500M of revenue from Richardson, Texas, and has crossed from franchisee to franchisor by acquiring Au Bon Pain.

Eyas Capital acquired BOJ of WNC — Bojangles' largest franchise group, 120 restaurants across six states — and immediately committed to more than 40 new units in Cincinnati and Columbus, taking its portfolio past 350 franchise units. Brentwood Associates and Sixth Street invested in Far West Services, the largest West Coast Wingstop franchisee at 127 locations. Guernsey Holdings, a multi-sector franchisee, bought 20 Zaxby's in South Carolina.

Sailormen entered 2026 with 136 Popeyes restaurants across Florida and Georgia, 3,300 employees and $233.5M of fiscal 2025 revenue. It filed Chapter 11 in January 2026 and sold 97 restaurants for $16.55M across five buyers. Read the per-restaurant pricing: Popeyes corporate paid roughly $600,000 per restaurant for 16 Miami units, 61 Biscuits about $370,000 per restaurant in West Palm Beach, and Pulse Restaurant Group about $54,000 per restaurant for 50 units across Tampa, Tallahassee, Pensacola and Jacksonville. Roughly 33 restaurants attracted no buyer.

Beneath the platforms, the most durable growth in chicken franchising comes from families redeploying capital between brands. The Korpal brothers, whose parents ran 22 Subway franchises in Southeast Texas, signed a 13-unit Golden Chick development agreement covering ten Houston units over four years and three in Beaumont. SXThree Restaurant Group operates 20 Golden Chicks in central Texas and is targeting 100 by 2030. Layne's added ten new franchisees in 2025, including operators from the Wendy's and Arby's systems.

Brand unit counts conceal almost everything that matters. Bojangles' footprint did not change when 120 of its restaurants passed from a founder-operator to an investment platform. KFC's closure count does not tell you which operator is absorbing the survivors. The chicken industry's real ownership map is held privately, updated through bankruptcy dockets, franchise transfers and development agreements — and that is precisely why it is worth building.

title: Chicken Expansion Outlook — 2026–2027
dek: More than 4,000 chicken restaurants are under some form of announced commitment. Not all of them will open.

sections.p: Adding up publicly announced development commitments across the brands CSW tracks produces a striking figure: Dave's Hot Chicken has roughly 1,000 locations in development and plans 150+ openings in 2026; Slim Chickens has a pipeline of more than 1,200 restaurants after signing 110 agreements in 2025; Church's plans 600 units in China and 900 across Europe and other international markets; Krispy Krunchy targets roughly 500 foodservice retrofit sites by 2030. Chick-fil-A expects 100+ new U.S. restaurants in 2026 and Raising Cane's nearly 100.

sections.h: Discount the agreements, respect the openings
sections.p: Signed area development agreements convert to open restaurants at well below 100% across franchising. The useful distinction is between committed pipeline and demonstrated throughput. Dave's opened eight restaurants in a single day in April 2026. Wingstop opened 102 restaurants in one quarter. Golden Chick set a brand record with 23 openings in 2025 and Layne's opened 21 while doubling its system. Those are throughput numbers. A 1,200-unit pipeline is an aspiration until sites are controlled.

sections.h: The geography is shifting north and east
sections.p: Zaxby's opened in the Bronx and on the Upper East Side after debuting in New Jersey in December 2025 — its 24th state. Bojangles is being built out in Ohio by Eyas Capital and in San Antonio under a 21-unit agreement. Slim Chickens is targeting Illinois, Ohio, Pennsylvania, New York, Massachusetts, New Jersey and Connecticut. Southeast chicken brands are, for the first time at scale, underwriting Northeast and Midwest real estate.

The binding constraint on chicken expansion in 2026–2027 is not capital or franchisee demand. It is site control and build cost. Huey Magoo's cut drive-thru build costs by roughly 40% and immediately became more franchisable. Slim Chickens hired a former Starbucks site-strategy executive as Chief Development Officer. Both moves are recognitions of the same reality: the brands with the pipeline are competing for the same pads, and whoever solves real estate throughput converts announcements into restaurants.
